e-568.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
e-568.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t) = 2t + 3t^2.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=1$ and $t=3?$
e-568.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}+{t}^{3})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[{3}^{2}+{3}^{3}]-[{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}] \\  & =[9+27]-[1+1] \\  & =36-2 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=1$ and $t=3$ is $34.$

e-7128.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
e-7128.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t) = 6t^2 +4t.$ At time $t=2$ the particle is located at the position $x=-20.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=4?$
e-7128.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=4$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in[2,4].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(4) = x(2) + \int_2^4 v(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(4) & =-20+{\int }_{2}^{4}(6{t}^{2}+4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & =-20+{[2{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-20+([2(4)^{3}+2(4)^{2}]-[2(2)^{3}+2(2)^{2}]) \\  & =-20+([128+32]-[16+8]) \\  & =-20+(160-24) \\  & =-20+136 \\  & =116.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=4$ is $x=116.$

e-7129.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t = 8$ is equal to its position at $t=2$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [2,8].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(8) = x(2)+ \int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm d t
$$

We are told that $x(2)=-1$, and we can compute the integral $\displaystyle\int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm dt$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=2$ to $t=8.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
\int_2^8 v(t) \, \textrm dt = 6.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(8) = -1+ 6 = 5
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=8$ is $x=5.$

after.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{3})+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})]}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+([-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3})]-[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{3})]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

content.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{3})+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})]}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+([-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3})]-[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{3})]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=2.$

$$
x(5)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(5) & =2{e}^{2}+{\int }_{1}^{5}3{e}^{3t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{2}+{[{e}^{3t-1}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2{e}^{2}+({e}^{3(5)-1}-{e}^{3(1)-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{2}+({e}^{14}-{e}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{2}+{e}^{14}-{e}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}+{e}^{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{2t+1}.$ At time $t=0.5$ the particle is located at the position $x={e}^{2}.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
after.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=0.5$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0.5,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(0.5)+{\int }_{0.5}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & ={e}^{2}+{\int }_{0.5}^{2}{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{2}+{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t+1}]}_{0.5}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(2)+1}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(0.5)+1}) \\  & ={e}^{2}+(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{5}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{5} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}+{e}^{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=\frac{{e}^{2}+{e}^{5}}{2}.$
